name: Papyrus 52
provenance: Bought in Egypt in 1920 by Bernard Grenfell | Identified and published by C. H. Roberts in 1935
condition: A single damaged leaf fragment, written on both sides
notes: Often called the earliest known fragment of a New Testament text; its date rests on handwriting alone.

name: Codex Alexandrinus
catalog_ids: Gregory–Aland A (02) | Royal MS 1 D V–VIII
contents: Most of the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) | Most of the New Testament | First Clement | Second Clement (incomplete)
provenance: Given by Cyril Lucaris, Patriarch of Constantinople, to King Charles I in 1627 | Came to the British Museum with the Royal Library in 1757
condition: Incomplete: leaves lost from Matthew, John and 2 Corinthians, and the end of Second Clement
notes: One of the four great uncial codices of the Greek Bible.

name: 4QJerb
repository: Israel Antiquities Authority (Dead Sea Scrolls collection)
date_text: 2nd century BC: the first half of the 2nd century BC, or the Hasmonaean period
provenance: Found in Qumran Cave 4 in 1952 | Published by Emanuel Tov in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XV (1997)
condition: Fragments of a scroll; part of the left side of a column survives
notes: In Jeremiah 10 it lacks verses 6–8 and 10, and places verse 9 within verse 5, as the Greek Septuagint does; the longer Masoretic Hebrew text has them. Scholars generally read it as a Hebrew witness to the shorter edition behind the Septuagint.

name: 4QJerd
repository: Israel Antiquities Authority (Dead Sea Scrolls collection)
date_text: 2nd century BC: the first half of the 2nd century BC, or the Hasmonaean period
provenance: Found in Qumran Cave 4 in 1952 | Published by Emanuel Tov in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XV (1997)
condition: A few small fragments of one column
notes: Its wording, including shorter forms of names in 43:4–6, is closer to the Septuagint's Jeremiah than to the longer Masoretic text; how far it agrees is still debated.

name: Papyrus 66
date_text: c. 200 (Victor Martin); estimates range from 100–150 to the 4th century
date_basis: palaeography (handwriting comparison); a later date argued from the book's format and construction
contents: Gospel of John 1:1–6:11 | John 6:35–21:9, with gaps
provenance: Found in 1952 at Jabal Abu Mana near Dishna, Egypt | Published in 1956
condition: Nearly complete for its first 26 leaves, with its binding stitching surviving; later leaves fragmentary
notes: One of the earliest near-complete copies of a Gospel; it does not contain John 7:53–8:11.

name: Papyrus 75
catalog_ids: Gregory–Aland 𝔓75 | P. Bodmer XIV–XV | Hanna Papyrus 1 (Mater Verbi)
date_text: Traditionally the 3rd century (175–225 by Martin and Kasser); later estimates reach the 4th century
contents: Gospel of Luke 3:18–24:53 (most of it) | Gospel of John 1:1–15:8
provenance: Found in Egypt in the 1950s, said to be at Pabau | Owned by Martin Bodmer | Sold in 2006 and given to the Vatican Library
condition: About 102 of some 144 pages survive, about 20 of them fragmentary
notes: The oldest known copy of Luke, and the earliest to hold Luke and John in one book.

name: Papyrus 46
catalog_ids: Gregory–Aland 𝔓46 | P. Chester Beatty II | P. Mich. inv. 6238
repository: Chester Beatty Library | University of Michigan
shelfmark: P. Chester Beatty II | P. Mich. inv. 6238
contents: Romans 9–16 | Hebrews | 1 and 2 Corinthians | Ephesians | Galatians | Philippians | Colossians | 1 Thessalonians (two chapters)
provenance: Of unknown origin in Egypt | Bought in parts by Alfred Chester Beatty and the University of Michigan | Published in full by Frederic Kenyon in 1934
condition: Every leaf has lost lines at its foot; the last seven leaves are missing
notes: The oldest surviving collection of Paul's letters; it places Hebrews straight after Romans.

name: Papyrus 45
catalog_ids: Gregory–Aland 𝔓45 | P. Chester Beatty I
contents: Matthew | John | Luke | Mark | Acts (portions of each, in that order)
provenance: Bought from a dealer by Alfred Chester Beatty | Published by Frederic Kenyon (1933–1958)
condition: About 30 fragmentary leaves survive of an original 110
notes: The earliest known book holding all four Gospels and Acts together.

name: Nash Papyrus
date_text: c. 150–100 BC (first dated to the 2nd century AD by Stanley Cook)
contents: The Ten Commandments, combining Exodus 20:2–17 and Deuteronomy 5:6–21 | The opening of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5)
provenance: Acquired in Egypt by W. L. Nash, reportedly from the Fayyum, in 1902 | Given to Cambridge University Library in 1903 | First described by Stanley Cook in 1903
condition: Twenty-four lines, with a few letters missing at each edge
notes: Before the Dead Sea Scrolls were found it was the oldest known manuscript of any part of the Hebrew Bible.

name: Papyrus of Ani
contents: The Book of the Dead (the Book of Coming Forth by Day), made for the Theban scribe Ani | Hymns to Ra and Osiris | The weighing of the heart, with Horus leading Ani to Osiris
size: c. 24 m long and 33 cm high
provenance: Taken from Ani's tomb at Thebes by dealers | Acquired by E. A. Wallis Budge for the British Museum in 1888
condition: Cut into sheets after it reached the museum
notes: Budge's translation of it (1895) is public domain; his Legends of the Gods (1912) is in the Library.

name: Papyrus Chester Beatty I (Egyptian)
date_text: c. 1147 BC, 20th Dynasty, reign of Ramesses V
date_basis: the reign named in the papyrus
contents: The Contendings of Horus and Seth | Love songs
provenance: From Thebes | Published by Alan Gardiner (Oxford University Press, 1931)
notes: The fullest surviving telling of the trial in which the gods decide between Horus and Seth for the throne of Osiris.
